title: Ang 785–792: Suhi ki Var
hookLine: Guru Amar Das's ballad, including the true sati, on ang 787
tomorrow: you saw the water rising. why didn't you build the raft?

cards: Scroll long enough and someone captions a couple photo "ride or die." It sounds romantic: loyalty so total you'd go down with them. In the Gurus' India, an old custom took that literally.

When a husband died, his widow was sometimes praised for joining him on the funeral fire, and she was called a sati, a faithful wife. It's a hard thing to hear, and the Guru doesn't look away from it.
On ang 787, in a ballad by Guru Amar Das, the word gets taken back.

teach.h: A BALLAD BY THE THIRD GURU.
teach.b: Suhi ki Var is the third Guru's ballad in raga Suhi: pauris, his own stanzas, each with saloks set before it. On ang 787, short saloks stand together.

teach.h: NOT THOSE WHO BURN WITH THE DEAD.
teach.b: The first, in paraphrase: they are not called sati who burn themselves with the dead. Nanak, a sati is one who dies from the blow of separation.
That's the soul missing the One it loves, the same longing as the bride in Suhi's wedding songs. Then the next salok widens it.
In paraphrase: they too are known as sati who live in modesty and contentment, who serve their Lord and rise each day to remember. Notice what the Guru did.
He took the most honored word for faithfulness in his world and moved it off the funeral fire and into ordinary days.

teach.h: FAITHFUL, ONE MORNING AT A TIME.
teach.b: Faithful isn't one dramatic act at the end. It's getting up again tomorrow. Decency, contentment, service and remembering, repeated.

Tradition remembers Guru Amar Das speaking against the custom itself; these saloks are the Granth's own words on it. Here's the line to tell someone tonight: in the Granth, a sati isn't a woman who died with her husband.
It's anyone, living, who stays true one morning at a time.

how: Ragis sing Suhi ki Var salok by salok and pauri by pauri; Sikhs often point to Guru Amar Das's saloks on ang 787 when they speak of the Gurus' stand on sati.

games.q: the saloks on ang 787 — tap the pairs.
p: those who burn with the dead

s: in the Granth, a sati is a widow who dies on the fire
ang 787 says the opposite: those who burn with the dead are not called sati.
Guru Amar Das's saloks say a living person can be a sati
those who live in modesty and contentment, serving and remembering each day, are called sati too.
'ride or die' loyalty is what the salok praises
it moves faithfulness off the dramatic end and into ordinary mornings.

games.q: your aunt has cared for your uncle since his stroke. she gets tired and short with him, and says she's failing him. by the saloks on ang 787, is she faithful?
o: yes: getting up and serving again each day is the faithful thing.
not yet: faithful means never feeling tired or short at all.
only if she gives up the rest of her life entirely for him.
games.why: the second salok names modesty, contentment, service and remembering, done day after day. tired and still there counts.

practice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper, and write one small, faithful thing you already do most days: a call, a chore, a prayer, a walk with someone. Hold the paper in your lap for the sit and let that ordinary thing count.
If you'd like, read the saloks on ang 787 first.

wordCard.voice: Ang 785. Where Suhi ki Var begins, Guru Amar Das's ballad, and two pages in, faithfulness rewritten.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sati, the faithful one; on ang 787 Guru Amar Das gives the name to the living.

carryVoice: Faithful: not one fire at the end, but a true thing done again each morning. That's the ballad's turn.
